title: Losing a job
hookLine: honest work lost, and the sangat helping
tomorrow: uncle's last paycheck came up short. speak up, or let it go?
last: A HARD WEEK, AND ITS LINES.

lines: A SIGN TAPED TO THE GLASS.
cards: Gurpreet uncle has driven for the same warehouse since before Simran was born. On Monday the doors have a printed sign taped to the glass: closed, effective today.
He comes over that night and sits at the kitchen table with his keys still in his hand, like he might need them. He doesn't say much. He keeps saying, I always worked.
Simran pours him tea and doesn't know what to do with her hands.

teach.b: In Sikhi, honest work is close to the center. Kirat karni, earning by your own effort, sits beside remembering the Name and sharing what you have.
On Ang 1245, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: one who eats what he earns by his labor, and gives some of it from his own hands, Nanak, that one knows the way.
Gurpreet uncle has lived both halves of that line, the earning and the giving.

teach.h: THE JOB ENDED, NOT HIS WORTH.
teach.b: Losing the job doesn't erase the kirat; the warehouse closed, not his worth. And now the giving comes back around, because a sangat is a lot of hands.
Harjit can't hire him right now, so he calls three other trucking companies before breakfast. Bebe, still on a walker, sends a container of dal home with him.
Simran sits with him at the laptop and fixes the résumé he hasn't touched in years. Nobody fixes it in a week.
But he isn't carrying the sign alone.

how: When someone loses work, Sikh families and sangats pass on job leads, help with applications, share meals, and sometimes help from daswandh, the tenth given for others.

o: a sign to stop working and rely on others
honest work ended, with your worth still whole
a punishment for not working hard enough

games.q: honest work, lost — tap the pairs.
p: earning by your own honest effort
earn by labor, give from your hands

s: in Sikhi, losing your job means losing your kirat
the warehouse closed, not his worth; the honest work he did still stands.
Guru Nanak links earning by labor with giving from your own hands
Ang 1245: that one knows the way.

games.q: a neighbor from another faith loses his job and says, 'i don't want charity.' what fits today?
o: offer what's useful: a lead, a ride, help with the résumé. he's not alone.
give him space; a proud man would rather handle it on his own.
send money quietly and say nothing, so it isn't awkward.
games.why: the sangat's help in the story isn't a handout: calls, dal, a résumé. not alone is something you do.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees and look at them for the whole sit: the palms, the knuckles, whatever work they've done.
If you pray, you can thank the Giver for the work they've had and ask for work for someone who's searching; if not, just look, and let the hands be honored.

wordCard.voice: Losing a job. Honest work ended, worth intact, and the sangat's hands reaching in.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest work, earning by one's own effort.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: not alone, because the hands that gave are met by hands. Two weeks of living it, done.

sources.ref: Ang 1245, Sarang ki Var, salok of Guru Nanak (ghaal khaae kichh hathahu dei, Nanak raahu pachhaanahi sei), paraphrased
